newsitem.title: UK: Fat and fit healthier than skinny, expert says.
newsitem.headline: Fat and fit healthier than skinny, expert says.

text.p: Being fit is more important for health than being thin, a U.S. researcher told a conference on Tuesday.
Obese people who are fit are less likely to die than thin people who do not exercise, Steven Blair, clinical director of the Cooper Institute for Aerobics Research, said.
He said he knew his research would be controversial, but it meant it could be more important to tell overweight people to exercise than to put them on a diet or on drugs.

"I know we are swimming upstream with this," Blair told the conference on Physical Activity and Healthy Weight Management, sponsored by Britain's Health Education Authority and the Association for the Study of Obesity.

"Thinness is fine if you want to be a swimsuit model. It's fine if you don't want to be discriminated against," Blair concluded. "But if you don't want to die, you're better off to be fit and have a big waist."
Blair's team studied 25,000 men and 7,000 women aged 20 to 88, with a mean age of 42.

They assessed their fitness levels in a laboratory and ranked the least fit one-third as unfit, the next third as moderately fit and the group best able to manage the treadmill test as very fit. Then they watched them for eight years.

Those who were the least fit were twice as likely to die as those who were moderately or very fit. The effect was the same when alcohol consumption, smoking, age, weight and other factors were taken into consideration.
The effect was also the same regardless of percentage body fat to muscle, total body fat or waist-to-hip ratio -- generally considered a measure of "high-risk" fat.
"The amount of fat that these men have does not matter," Blair said. "What matters is whether they are fit or unfit."
Even the "men with big bellies" had a lower death rate if they were fit than thin, unfit men, Blair found. He said he hoped other researchers would try to duplicate his findings.
Wim Saris of the University of Maastricht in the Netherlands said exercise was proved to burn off fat and helped counteract the bad effects of dieting -- such as a lowered metabolic rate.
It also seemed to change people's appetites -- causing them to choose healthier foods, he said.
Blair said the amount of exercise needed to be "moderately fit" by his team's standards was modest. Walking briskly for half an hour a day -- about two miles (3.2 km) worth -- would do it, he said.
"You do not have to be an athlete," he added. "You just have to get out of the bottom -- you have to get out of the couch potato category."

But this is the hard part, Peter Fentem and Simon Mockett of the University of Nottingham told the conference. "Few older people report walking at a fairly brisk or fast pace for half an hour," they said.
Only three percent of older British men -- those over 55 -- walked regularly and only two percent of women.
One British survey showed that almost half of all inactive people said they did not exercise because they "were not the sporty type", Stuart Biddle of the University of Exeter said.
"It is not surprising that there is a belief among professionals that exercise motivation is very difficult for overweight people," he told the conference.
Obesity is linked with diabetes, heart disease and early death. Nearly 14 percent of men and 17 percent of women in Britain are obese, with even higher percentages in Germany and the United States.
"Clearly, overweight represents one of the most serious threats to public health," Ken Fox of Exeter University and the conference organiser, said.
